title: SHOULD CHRISTIANS COMMAND ANGELS? THE DANGEROUS SPIRITUAL MISTAKE THAT SOUNDS LIKE FAITH BUT MAY BE STEALING OUR ATTENTION FROM JESUS
paragraphs: SHOULD CHRISTIANS COMMAND ANGELS? THE DANGEROUS SPIRITUAL MISTAKE THAT SOUNDS LIKE FAITH BUT MAY BE STEALING OUR ATTENTION FROM JESUS

Angels are real. Spiritual warfare is real. God's protection is real. But somewhere between believing in heavenly protection and claiming authority over heavenly beings, a dangerous confusion has entered Christian teaching. And the truth hidden in Scripture may change the way you pray forever.
Imagine standing beside your child's hospital bed at two in the morning.
The machines are beeping. The doctors have done what they can. Your child is asleep, but you cannot close your eyes.
You have prayed until your throat hurts.
You have whispered the name of Jesus so many times that the words are almost indistinguishable from your breathing.
And then you remember something a preacher once told you.
"You have authority over angels. Command them to go. Dispatch them into the hospital. Order them to fight for your child."
So you stand up.
You stretch out your trembling hands.
And you begin issuing commands to heaven.
But what if, in the middle of your desperation, someone had taught you to exercise an authority Scripture never actually gave you?
What if God truly has angels watching over His children, but He never instructed His children to become their commanders?

And what if the greatest power available to you in that hospital room was never your ability to give orders to angels, but your privilege of approaching the throne of Almighty God through Jesus Christ?
Please stay with me.
Because this is not an article denying angels.
It is not an attack on Christians who have prayed this way.
And it is certainly not an attempt to diminish the supernatural power of God.
It is about something far more serious.
The difference between trusting the authority of Jesus and claiming an authority Jesus never promised us.
And that difference matters more than many believers realize.
There is something deeply comforting about knowing we are not alone.
When life becomes unbearable, when the diagnosis arrives, when the marriage collapses, when the enemy seems to be attacking everything we love, we want to know that heaven is moving.
We want to believe that unseen armies are standing between us and destruction.
And Scripture gives us genuine reasons for confidence.
Psalm 34:7 declares:
"The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them."
Psalm 91:11 says:
"For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways."
Notice those words.
"He shall give his angels charge."
Not you shall give His angels charge.
He.
God.
That distinction is not a small grammatical technicality. It reveals who possesses the authority being exercised.
In the Hebrew of Psalm 91:11, the expression is:
כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה־לָּךְ
Ki mal'akhav yetsavveh-lakh.
A careful rendering is:
"For He will command His angels concerning you."
The verb יְצַוֶּה (yetsavveh) comes from the Hebrew root צוה (tsavah), meaning to command, charge, or give an order.
The subject of that command is God.
The angels belong to Him.
The orders come from Him.
And the protection is His gracious provision.
Do you see how beautiful that actually is?
Your safety does not depend upon whether you have mastered the right spiritual vocabulary.
It does not depend upon whether you know the names of particular angels.
It does not depend upon whether you can shout commands with enough intensity to make heaven respond.
Your confidence rests in the God who neither slumbers nor sleeps.
And sometimes the most powerful prayer you can offer is not an elaborate declaration.
Sometimes it is simply:
"Father, I am afraid. Please help me."
There is no shame in that prayer.
There is no weakness in that surrender.
There is no spiritual inferiority in a believer who cries out to God rather than attempting to direct the inhabitants of heaven.
In fact, that posture of dependence may be much closer to biblical faith than the confident commands circulating through certain Christian teachings.
But someone may object.
"Didn't Jesus give us authority?"
Yes.
Absolutely.
And we must never diminish what Jesus actually gave His followers.
In Luke 10:19, Jesus told the seventy-two disciples He had sent out that He had given them authority over the power of the enemy.
In Luke 10:17, those disciples returned rejoicing that even demons were subject to them in His name.
But listen carefully to what Jesus said next.
Luke 10:20:
"Notwithstanding in this rejoice not, that the spirits are subject unto you; but rather rejoice, because your names are written in heaven."
What a breathtaking correction.
The disciples were celebrating spiritual authority.
Jesus redirected their joy toward salvation.
They were amazed by what submitted to them.
Jesus wanted them to rejoice in the grace that had received them.
He was not denying the authority He had given.
He was teaching them where their deepest security belonged.
And here is the distinction we cannot afford to ignore.
Authority over demonic spirits is not the same thing as authority over God's holy angels.
Those are different categories of spiritual beings, and Scripture does not permit us to collapse them into one.
Jesus authorized His disciples to confront demonic opposition in His name.
But where does He instruct ordinary believers to summon, dispatch, command, or assign missions to holy angels?
That is the question.
And a teaching should not be established merely because it sounds powerful.
It must be established by the Word of God.
Consider Hebrews 1:14:
"Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?"
The original Greek reads:
οὐχὶ πάντες εἰσὶν λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα εἰς διακονίαν ἀποστελλόμενα διὰ τοὺς μέλλοντας κληρονομεῖν σωτηρίαν;
A faithful translation is:
"Are they not all ministering spirits being sent out for service for the sake of those who are about to inherit salvation?"
Two Greek expressions deserve our attention.
λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα (leitourgika pneumata) means "ministering spirits."
ἀποστελλόμενα (apostellomena) means "being sent out."
The passage beautifully affirms that angels serve God's saving purposes on behalf of His people.
But it does not identify believers as the ones issuing their orders.
The broader context of Hebrews 1 is especially important.
The chapter is not primarily explaining how Christians should interact with angels.
It is declaring the absolute superiority of Jesus Christ over angels.
The Son is greater.
The Son is enthroned.
The Son receives the honor that belongs to Him.
The angels are servants.
Jesus is Lord.
And if we read a passage written to exalt Christ but walk away fascinated mainly by the possibility of controlling angels, we have missed its central message.
Think about that for a moment.
A chapter designed to magnify Jesus can be misused to magnify our supposed spiritual rank.
That should concern us.
Not because angels are unimportant.
But because no spiritual experience should become more precious to us than the Savior Himself.
And there is a passage that makes this even more sobering.
Jude 9 describes a dispute involving Michael the archangel and the devil.
The verse says:
"Yet Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee."
Read that last sentence again.
"The Lord rebuke thee."
Michael is no ordinary angel.
He is explicitly called an archangel.
Yet in this account, he appeals to the Lord's authority rather than pronouncing a reviling judgment on his own initiative.
Now we must interpret this responsibly.
Jude 9 does not directly address whether Christians may command angels. It concerns Michael's response during a dispute with the devil.
But it does provide a striking biblical example of restraint and reverence for divine authority.
If even Michael's response is presented in this manner, we should be cautious about developing a spirituality built around extravagant declarations of our own authority.
And there is something else.
The apostle Paul warns in Colossians 2:18 against practices involving the worship of angels and claims to extraordinary spiritual experiences.
The Greek phrase θρησκείᾳ τῶν ἀγγέλων (thrēskeia tōn angelōn) is commonly understood in this context as referring to angel worship, although scholars have discussed nuances of the expression.
Paul's warning is not a blanket prohibition against acknowledging angelic ministry.
It is a warning against religious practices that draw believers away from their proper dependence upon Christ.
And Colossians 2:19 identifies the deeper problem.
Not holding fast to the Head.
Christ Himself.
That is the danger.
Not that a believer might believe too strongly in angels.
But that a believer might become so absorbed in angelic activity that the sufficiency and supremacy of Jesus slowly fade into the background.
It can happen almost without anyone noticing.
A person begins by praying for protection.
Then someone introduces the idea of assigning angels to family members.
Soon they are being taught to command angels over their finances, businesses, vehicles, homes, and relationships.
Eventually, their spiritual confidence becomes tied to whether they have successfully activated the right heavenly assistance.
And somewhere along the way, prayer can begin to resemble a technique for controlling the unseen world rather than communion with a loving Father.
But beloved, heaven is not a machine.
Angels are not spiritual employees waiting for our instructions.
And the name of Jesus is not a magical formula that grants us unrestricted command over whatever spiritual beings we choose to address.
The name of Jesus represents the authority and person of the risen Lord.
It is not a substitute for submitting to His will.
Even when Jesus taught His disciples to pray, He directed them toward the Father.
"Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name."
And then:
"Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven."
Matthew 6:9–10.
Not my kingdom.
Not my will.
Not my instructions imposed upon heaven.
Your will be done.
There is a kind of spiritual maturity that stops trying to sound powerful and begins learning how to trust the One who truly is powerful.
And perhaps that is what some of us desperately need.
Because underneath our desire to command angels, there may be something deeply human.
Fear.
We are afraid of losing the people we love.
Afraid of another financial collapse.
Afraid of a disease returning.
Afraid of another betrayal.
Afraid that if we do not pray correctly, something terrible might happen.
So when someone offers a teaching that makes us feel more in control, it can become incredibly attractive.
Especially when life has already made us feel helpless.
But what if the answer to your fear is not greater control?
What if the answer is greater confidence in the character of God?
There is a moment in 2 Kings 6 that I wish every frightened Christian could see.
Elisha's servant wakes up and discovers that enemy forces have surrounded the city.
Horses.
Chariots.
An army.
There appears to be no escape.
The servant panics.
And Elisha says:
"Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them."
Then Elisha prays.
Notice what he does not do.
He does not begin assigning individual angels to strategic positions.
He does not issue instructions to heavenly chariots.
He prays to the Lord.
"Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see."
And God opens the servant's eyes.
The mountain is full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha.
The heavenly forces were already there.
Before the servant could see them.
Before he understood what God was doing.
Before he had any idea how he would survive.
God had not abandoned them.
And there is a word here for the person who is exhausted from trying to hold everything together.
You do not have to command what God already governs.
You do not have to supervise heaven for God to remember your address.
You do not have to become an expert in angelic ranks before your prayers matter.
Your Father knows.
Your Savior intercedes.
Your life is not hidden from His sight.
That does not mean every crisis will end the way we desperately want.
Christians still suffer.
Faithful believers still become ill.
Families still grieve.
And sometimes God's deliverance looks very different from the miracle we pleaded to receive.
The Bible never promises that angelic protection will eliminate every earthly tragedy.
Indeed, the devil himself quoted Psalm 91 when tempting Jesus to throw Himself from the temple.
Matthew 4:5–7 records that temptation.
Satan used a genuine promise about angelic protection to encourage an act of presumption.
Jesus answered with Scripture:
"Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God."
That should make us tremble.
A verse about God's protection can be twisted into a demand that God prove Himself on our terms.
And if Jesus refused to manipulate a divine promise into a spectacle, why would we build our spiritual lives around doing something similar?
God's promises invite trust.
They do not authorize presumption.
But perhaps you are wondering about another passage.
Didn't Jesus say He could ask His Father for twelve legions of angels?
Yes.
In Matthew 26:53, during His arrest, Jesus said:
"Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels?"
Think about the setting.
Jesus was being betrayed.
Armed men had come to seize Him.
One of His disciples had drawn a sword.
And Jesus declared that heavenly assistance was available to Him.
Yet He did not call those angels to prevent His arrest.
He willingly submitted to the Father's redemptive purpose.
The Son of God could have escaped.
But He stayed.
Not because He lacked power.
Not because heaven was unwilling.
But because love was carrying Him toward the cross.
And this is where the conversation about angels becomes something much greater.
Because the deepest Christian question is not:
"How can I get angels to do what I want?"
It is:
"How can I become more like Jesus, who surrendered Himself completely to the Father's will?"
At Calvary, the One whom angels worship allowed sinful human beings to mock Him.
The One through whom all things were created permitted His hands to be pierced.
The One who possessed all authority refused to abandon the mission of redemption.
He did not come merely to demonstrate supernatural power.
He came to save sinners.
He came for the ashamed.
The rebellious.
The religious pretenders.
The people who had made a wreck of their lives.
The people who had confused spiritual performance with intimacy with God.
The people who knew how to speak Christian language but had forgotten how to surrender.
He came for people like us.
And the scandal of the cross is that the holy Son of God suffered for the unholy.
The innocent died for the guilty.
The righteous One gave Himself for sinners.
Then, on the third day, He rose again.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
Our failures did not have the final word.
Jesus Christ did.
And suddenly, the question of whether we can command angels seems much smaller beside the staggering reality that, through Christ, sinners can approach the throne of grace.
Hebrews 4:16 says:
"Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need."
Come boldly.
Not because you possess independent authority over the heavenly host.
But because Jesus is our great High Priest.
Because His sacrifice is sufficient.
Because mercy is available through Him.
Because the door that sin had closed has been opened by His blood.
Do you understand what that means?
You may not have biblical authorization to command Michael.
You may not have biblical authorization to dispatch Gabriel.
But through Jesus Christ, you are invited to approach the Father Himself.
Why would we trade that privilege for an authority Scripture has not clearly given us?
And please hear this with tenderness.
If you have spent years commanding angels because you genuinely believed you were obeying Scripture, this is not an invitation to drown in condemnation.
Many sincere Christians have repeated teachings they received from people they trusted.
The issue is not whether we have ever misunderstood a passage.
Every one of us has more to learn.
The issue is what we do when Scripture challenges something we have believed.
Will we defend a familiar practice simply because it makes us feel powerful?
Or will we humble ourselves before the Word of God?
Acts 17:11 commends the Bereans for examining the Scriptures daily to see whether the things they were hearing were true.
That is the spirit we need.
Not mockery.
Not pride.
Not endless arguments in comment sections.
But a genuine willingness to be corrected by God's Word.

Some Christians distinguish between commanding angels and asking God to send angels, while others believe speaking to angels can be an expression of delegated authority. Those distinctions deserve careful consideration rather than careless caricature.
Yet the biblical examples and instructions examined here provide strong grounds for a clear, responsible conclusion:
Christians can confidently ask God for angelic protection and assistance, but Scripture does not clearly authorize believers to issue commands directly to God's holy angels.
That is not unbelief.
That is biblical restraint.
And biblical restraint can be an expression of deep faith.
When Peter was imprisoned in Acts 12, the church prayed earnestly to God for him.
God sent an angel to deliver Peter.
The church prayed.
God acted.
The angel served.
The glory belonged to the Lord.
What a beautiful pattern.
And when Jesus was in Gethsemane, Luke 22:43 records an angel from heaven strengthening Him, although this verse has a recognized textual variant in the manuscript tradition.
Even in that scene of agony, the focus remains on Jesus' surrender to the Father.
"Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done."
Luke 22:42.
There is something here that our generation desperately needs to recover.
We have become fascinated with declarations.
Declarations of breakthrough.
Declarations of victory.
Declarations of protection.
Declarations of authority.
Some of these can express biblical truth when properly understood.
But sometimes we have become so concerned with speaking as though we control outcomes that we have forgotten how to kneel before the God who does.
Faith is not measured by how forcefully we speak to invisible beings.
Faith is measured by its object.
And the object of saving Christian faith is Jesus Christ.
Not angels.
Not spiritual techniques.
Not the intensity of our voices.
Jesus.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who holds all authority in heaven and on earth.
The One before whom every knee will bow.
The One who will never be displaced from His throne.
Maybe you have been praying for protection over your family.
Keep praying.
Maybe you are facing spiritual opposition.
Stand firm in Christ.
Put on the whole armor of God described in Ephesians 6.
Resist the devil, as James 4:7 instructs, while first submitting yourself to God.
Maybe you are terrified of what tomorrow might bring.
Bring that fear to your Father.
Ask Him to guard your home.
Ask Him to protect your children.
Ask Him to send whatever help He knows you need, including angelic assistance if that is His will.
There is nothing wrong with trusting God to employ His angels according to His purposes.
But let Him be the Commander.
Let Jesus remain the center.
Let the Holy Spirit lead you into truth.
And let your prayers become expressions of trust rather than attempts to control heaven.
Perhaps your prayer tonight can be as simple as this:

"Father, forgive me for the times I have been more fascinated by spiritual power than by Your presence. Forgive me for repeating teachings without examining Your Word. Thank You for Your angels, for Your protection, and for the unseen ways You care for Your children. But above all, thank You for Jesus. Teach me to trust Your authority instead of inventing my own. Guard my family according to Your wisdom. Strengthen me in spiritual battles. And when I cannot understand what You are doing, help me remember that You are still good. In the name of Jesus Christ, amen."
And now I want to ask you something personal.
Not as a test of how much Scripture you know.
Not as an invitation to attack a preacher, ministry, or denomination.
But as a moment of spiritual honesty.
Have you ever confused being spiritually powerful with being spiritually surrendered?
Have you ever felt afraid that if you did not say the right words, God might not protect you?
Have you ever been so consumed with spiritual warfare that you forgot the peace of simply belonging to Jesus?
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not alone.
Someone may find the courage to return to prayer after years of confusion.
Someone may realize that spiritual maturity is not about sounding impressive.
It is about becoming more faithful to Christ.
And if you know a Christian who has been taught to command angels, please do not send this article as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
Because this ministry is not about building fascination around angels.
It is about pointing people to Christ.
And that brings me to something important.
Every day, people are searching for answers.
Some are quietly losing their faith.
Some have been wounded by spiritual manipulation.
Some are trapped in religious confusion.
Some are desperately trying to understand what the Bible actually says.
And some are one honest, Scripture-centered message away from opening their hearts again to the truth of the Gospel.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
To keep pointing people beyond spiritual noise, beyond shallow inspiration, and beyond fear-based religion toward the person and finished work of Jesus Christ.
We want biblical nourishment to remain accessible to people who cannot afford expensive resources.
But continuing and expanding this work requires faithful support.

It can be part of your Christian generosity and stewardship, but it should never be confused with a biblical requirement to tithe to this particular ministry, nor should it replace your responsibility to discern how God would have you support your local church and other legitimate needs.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Not guilt.
Not fear.
Only an invitation to participate in work you believe is faithful and worthwhile.
It is the opportunity to help keep Christ-centered biblical teaching and discipleship resources reaching people who need them.
You can pray.
You can invite your family and friends to read it.
You can help make free discipleship resources known to people who would otherwise never discover them.
Your worth before God is not measured by your ability to contribute financially.
It is Christ who saves, Christ who sustains, and Christ who deserves the glory.
And before you leave, I want to return to that hospital room.
The frightened parent.
The sleeping child.
The trembling hands.
The desperate need for heaven to intervene.
Imagine that parent slowly lowering those hands.
Not because faith has disappeared.
But because something has become clear.
They do not need to control the angels.
They need to trust the Father.
They can pray for healing.
They can ask for protection.
They can plead for mercy.
They can seek medical help, receive support, and surrender their deepest fears to God.
And whatever happens next, they can know that their prayers are heard through Jesus Christ.
Not because they discovered a secret command.
But because the Savior has opened the way to the Father.
That is the Gospel.
We were separated from God by sin.
We could not rescue ourselves.
No angel could atone for our rebellion.
No spiritual declaration could erase our guilt.
No religious performance could make us righteous.
So Jesus came.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose victorious.
And He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where our hope begins.
That is where our confidence belongs.
And that is where every teaching about angels must ultimately lead us.
Back to Jesus.
Always back to Jesus.
Because the greatest miracle is not that heaven sends angels to serve God's children.
The greatest miracle is that the Son of God came to save His enemies and make them His family.
And when that truth finally reaches the deepest part of your soul, you begin to understand something unforgettable.
You were never asked to command heaven's armies. You were invited to know heaven's King.
